issues.legal_issue: A magistrate’s authority to direct further police investigation after taking cognizance, issuing process, and the accused appearing in response is limited when the request comes from the informant rather than the investigating agency.
material_facts: The police filed a report, the court took cognizance, charges were framed, and the accused appeared and stood trial.

After the informant’s and investigating officer’s evidence had been recorded and the accused had made their statements, the informant sought further investigation at the stage when the case was fixed for final arguments.
The informant sought forensic examination of a disputed page in a notary’s register; the investigating agency had not requested further investigation.
The trial court allowed the request, but the High Court set aside its order.
issues.conclusion: After cognizance has been taken, process issued, and the accused appeared, the magistrate cannot direct further investigation suo motu or on the informant’s request. At that stage, further investigation may be directed only on the investigating agency’s request and where material evidence warrants it to secure a fair investigation and trial. The appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 173(8) of the Code of Criminal Procedure authorizes the investigating agency to conduct further investigation after filing its report and to submit a further report; the provision does not confer the same post-cognizance power on the magistrate once the accused has appeared. Sections 156(3) and 190 permit investigation and cognizance at the pre-cognizance stage; investigation under Section 202 is an inquiry to assist the magistrate in deciding whether to proceed, not further investigation under Section 173(8). Sections 311 and 319 provide trial-stage powers to secure relevant evidence and proceed against other persons. The court relied on, among other authorities, Ram Lal Narang v. State (Delhi Administration), Randhir Singh Rana v. State (Delhi Administration), Reeta Nag v. State of West Bengal, Vinay Tyagi v. Irshad Ali, and Bhagwant Singh v. Commissioner of Police. It distinguished pre-cognizance decisions such as Bhagwant Singh and Chandra Babu alias Moses v. State.

rule.if: trial_after_police_report and cognizance_taken and accused_appeared and informant_requests_further_investigation and not investigating_agency_requests_further_investigation

predicates.trial_after_police_report: A criminal trial is proceeding after police have filed a report on their investigation.
predicates.cognizance_taken: The court has taken cognizance of the alleged offence on the basis of the police report.
predicates.accused_appeared: The accused have appeared in response to process issued by the court.
predicates.informant_requests_further_investigation: The informant asks the court to direct further police investigation.
predicates.investigating_agency_requests_further_in: The investigating agency asks the court to permit or direct further investigation.
predicates.magistrate_cannot_direct_further_investi: The magistrate is not permitted to direct further police investigation.

issues.definition: When a criminal trial following a police report is underway after cognizance and the accused have appeared, an informant’s request alone does not permit the magistrate to direct further investigation.

issues.legal_issue: A request for further investigation made at the close of a trial may be rejected when it is substantially delayed despite an earlier opportunity to raise it and no defective investigation is shown.
material_facts: The informant’s evidence was recorded more than two years before he sought further investigation, giving him an earlier opportunity to examine the disputed register page.
The request was made after the accused’s statements had been recorded, when the matter was fixed for final arguments.
The High Court found that the informant had offered no adequate explanation for the delay and that the circumstances did not show a defective investigation requiring further inquiry.
The investigating officer had seized the entire notary register; the High Court considered that any suspicious feature in it would have been examined.
issues.conclusion: Independently of the magistrate’s lack of authority to grant the informant’s request, the delayed application at the closing stage of the trial was not entertainable on these facts.
issues.legal_principle: The court endorsed the High Court’s fact-specific assessment that the request was made after a substantial, unexplained delay despite an earlier opportunity, and that the record did not demonstrate a defective investigation calling for further inquiry. The court cited no separate statutory test or earlier case as the basis for this alternative conclusion.

rule.if: trial_after_police_report and informant_had_earlier_opportunity and request_made_at_trial_end and request_substantially_delayed_without_explanation and no_defective_investigation_shown

predicates.trial_after_police_report: A criminal trial is proceeding after police have filed a report on their investigation.
predicates.informant_had_earlier_opportunity: The informant previously had an opportunity to examine the material later relied on to seek further investigation.
predicates.request_made_at_trial_end: The informant seeks further investigation when the trial is at its closing stage.
predicates.request_substantially_delayed_without_ex: The informant makes the request after substantial delay without an adequate explanation for waiting.
predicates.no_defective_investigation_shown: The circumstances do not show a defect in the investigation requiring further inquiry.
predicates.late_request_not_entertainable: The court does not entertain the delayed request for further investigation.

issues.definition: A request made at the close of a criminal trial is not entertained when the informant had an earlier opportunity, delayed substantially without explanation, and has not shown a defective investigation.
